cards.b:
Some books add more traditional approaches.

Comparative approach

Aristotle compared 158 constitutions. Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), compared laws across countries and linked them to climate, religion and customs. Bryce compared modern democracies.

Sociological approach

Studies how society shapes politics, as Montesquieu and later Tocqueville did in Democracy in America (1835–40).

Psychological approach

Graham Wallas, in Human Nature in Politics (1908), argued people act on instinct and emotion more than reason. This prepared the ground for behaviouralism.

These bridge the old and the new: they stay value-based, but begin to look at how politics actually works.

cards.b:
Indian political science took up behavioural methods from the 1960s.

  • The Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS) was founded in Delhi in 1963 by Rajni Kothari.
  • Its Lokniti programme runs the National Election Studies, large surveys of how Indians vote.
  • Kothari's Politics in India (1970) used systems ideas to describe the "Congress system".

But Indian scholars also showed the limits of imported models. Western theories predicted that modernisation would weaken caste. Instead, Rudolph and Rudolph in The Modernity of Tradition (1967) showed caste associations adapting to democracy.

This is a classic post-behavioural point: methods must be fitted to local reality.

cards.h: Groups, cross-cutting ties and polyarchy in practice
cards.b:
Pluralists built their theory on studies of interest groups.

  • Arthur Bentley, in The Process of Government (1908), said politics is nothing but the pressure of groups on one another.
  • David Truman, in The Governmental Process (1951), added the idea of overlapping membership. A person can be a worker, a Catholic and a parent at once, so groups cannot become too extreme.
  • Truman also spoke of potential groups: when an interest is threatened, people organise. This keeps the system balanced.

The upshot is a state that acts like a weather vane or broker, responding to whichever group pressures are strongest.

Critics say this is too rosy. E.E. Schattschneider famously wrote that the flaw in the pluralist heaven is that the heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent.

cards.h: Other Indian readings of the state
cards.b:
Pranab Bardhan

In The Political Economy of Development in India (1984), he named three dominant proprietary classes: industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats. They compete for state subsidies, which slows growth.

Rajni Kothari

Described the decline of the Congress system and the rise of a more centralised, personalised state from the 1970s.

Atul Kohli

In State-Directed Development (2004), he called India a fragmented-multiclass state, less effective than South Korea's cohesive-capitalist state.

Sudipta Kaviraj

Read Indian state-building as a passive revolution led by bourgeois and bureaucratic elites.

cards.b:
Later feminists asked: which women does feminism speak for?

Chandra Talpade Mohanty

In "Under Western Eyes" (1984/1986), she criticised Western feminists for treating "Third World women" as one passive, oppressed victim group.

Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak

In "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), she used the British ban on sati to show how both colonisers and local elites spoke for subaltern women, never letting them speak.

bell hooks

In Ain't I a Woman (1981), she showed how racism and sexism combine for Black women.

These ideas feed into intersectionality: the state treats a poor Dalit woman differently from a rich upper-caste woman, so gender alone cannot explain her position.
